content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Baby in the Water
objectives: I can follow baby Moses (pbuh) from the order to kill boys to his name in the palace.
I can explain why the writer uses the passive for what happens to the baby.
I can explain the Nile and Red Sea parallel without mixing the two events.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose why the writer uses the passive (to keep attention on the baby and the basket), then correct three verb forms: “was found”, “was given”, and “took place”, which has no passive. The last activity asks you to explain the Nile and Red Sea parallel.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: MU-sa, COP-tic. Stress: mi-RAC-u-lous-ly, sal-VA-tion, REG-u-lar-ly, com-bi-NA-tion. Say the meanings clearly: “mu” water, “sa” tree.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Water and Tree”. Which two words make the name Musa? Listen once and follow the baby from danger to the palace. Read again and mark every passive (was placed, was set free, was found, was given).
discussionPoints: A basket on a river carried a baby into the palace of the ruler who wanted him dead. Why do stories often show safety coming from the place of greatest danger?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Basket on the Nile” and “Water and Tree”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again from “In Moses’ (pbuh) time”. Number each event as it appears: the order, the basket, the tree, the palace. Ask where the baby was when he got his name, then order again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–5 sentences explaining the Nile and Red Sea parallel. Use one passive form and one contrast or time marker such as later, while or whereas, and keep the two events separate.

whatToNotice: The chapter ends by linking two waters: The Nile that carried the baby to the palace and the Red Sea where Moses (pbuh) and his people were later saved. This link is the writer’s own framing.
Notice “He was placed in a basket and the basket was set free on the waters of the Nile.” The passive keeps the focus on the baby and the basket; it does not mean that nobody acted.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Water and Tree”. Which two words make the name Musa?
Listen once and follow the baby from danger to the palace.
Read again and mark every passive (was placed, was set free, was found, was given).
Open the picture hotspots “A Basket on the Nile” and “Water and Tree” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find the Pharaoh’s worry and what he regularly ordered.
Middle: Find where the basket was found and how the baby was saved.
Last sentences: Find the meaning of the name and the two waters the writer links.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: miraculously, salvation, regularly, combination, banks.
“The salvation of Prophet Moses (pbuh) and his people from the Pharaoh also took place in waters, in the Red Sea.” Which word tells you the writer is linking two events?
Write one sentence with regularly and one with combination.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order four events. Follow the chapter from the beginning to the middle, and ask when the name could be given.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again from “In Moses’ (pbuh) time”.
Number each event as it appears: the order, the basket, the tree, the palace.
Ask where the baby was when he got his name, then order again.
selfCheck: Can I retell how the baby reached the palace?
Can I explain why the passive is used?
Can I explain why “was taken place” is wrong?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–5 sentences explaining the Nile and Red Sea parallel. Use one passive form and one contrast or time marker such as later, while or whereas, and keep the two events separate.
content.reflectionPrompt: A basket on a river carried a baby into the palace of the ruler who wanted him dead. Why do stories often show safety coming from the place of greatest danger?

objectives: I can describe the Pharaoh’s absolute power and how people behaved under it.
I can keep each claim with its source: the writer, Ibn Abbas, or the priests and magicians.
I can report a vision and a prediction with said that, had seen and would be.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort phrases into what people showed in public and what some held in private, correct “It is possible that” (not certain) and “made the Children of Israel work” (no to), then report the vision and the prediction with had seen and would be. The last activity asks you to report a dream or prediction carefully.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: ibn AB-bas, je-RU-sa-lem. Stress: PA-gan-ism, OUT-ward-ly, VI-sion, dis-HON-or. Read “It is possible that …” in a lighter, more careful voice than the sentences around it.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Pharaoh’s Dream”. What did the Pharaoh see? Listen once and count the voices in the chapter. Read again and mark It is possible that, Ibn Abbas said and They said.
discussionPoints: Some people hid what they believed because they were weak. What does it cost a person to live one way in public and another way in private?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A King Who Called Himself God” and “The Pharaoh’s Dream”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one person or group at a time. Find the sentence where that person speaks or is described. Keep the writer’s careful words with the silent people, then match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–6 sentences reporting a dream or prediction from a source. Attribute the report, use said that or another reporting verb, and keep the prediction apart from an established fact.

whatToNotice: The chapter has several voices: The narrator describes the Pharaoh, the writer carefully guesses about hidden believers, Ibn Abbas reports the vision, and the priests and magicians predict.
Notice “It is possible that some people of that period did not practise or believe in paganism.” The writer does not claim this as certain; it is a careful possibility.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Pharaoh’s Dream”. What did the Pharaoh see?
Listen once and count the voices in the chapter.
Read again and mark It is possible that, Ibn Abbas said and They said.
Open the picture hotspots “A King Who Called Himself God” and “The Pharaoh’s Dream” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find how the Pharaoh ruled and how he treated the Children of Israel.
Middle: Find what some people kept secret, how they behaved outwardly and why.
Last sentences: Find what the fire in the vision did and what the priests and magicians said.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: norms, outwardly, vision, paganism, dishonor.
“But they kept it secret and outwardly followed social norms without opposing the Pharaoh or telling who they were because they were weak.” What is the gap between their public and private lives?
Write one sentence with outwardly and one with norms.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four people or groups with what the chapter reports about them. The middle of the chapter covers the Pharaoh and the silent people; the end covers the vision and its meaning.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one person or group at a time.
Find the sentence where that person speaks or is described.
Keep the writer’s careful words with the silent people, then match again.
selfCheck: Can I say who reports the vision?
Can I explain why It is possible that is careful?
Can I report “A boy will be born” after they said?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–6 sentences reporting a dream or prediction from a source. Attribute the report, use said that or another reporting verb, and keep the prediction apart from an established fact.
content.reflectionPrompt: Some people hid what they believed because they were weak. What does it cost a person to live one way in public and another way in private?

content.chapter: Chapter 6: A Baby in the Nile
objectives: I can explain why the Pharaoh changed his order and what the new policy was.
I can contrast the Pharaoh’s economic calculation with the mother’s trust.
I can link cause, result and fear with because, so and for fear that.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four parts of the Qur’anic words with what each does (a condition and action, a comforting prohibition, a promise of return, a promise about his future), then complete three lines with because, so and for fear. The last activity asks you to explain a difficult decision.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: POL-i-cy, RE-al-is-tic, EX-perts, GRIEVE. Read the Qur’anic words slowly: pause after “put him into the river” and give “fear not, nor grieve” a calm, even tone.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Killing Every Other Year”. How did the new policy work? Listen once for the two decisions. Read again and mark because, so and for fear that.
discussionPoints: The Pharaoh spared boys for economic reasons, not mercy. How can a decision look kinder than it is when we do not ask why it was made?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Killing Every Other Year” and “A Mother’s Trust”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the first five sentences. Find what the economic experts warned the Pharaoh about. Choose the option that names the reason in those sentences, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences about a difficult decision. Use one cause, one when or if condition, one instruction and one future reassurance, so that the sentences form a sequence.

whatToNotice: The chapter sets two decisions side by side: The Pharaoh’s policy, judged “economically realistic”, and the mother’s act of trust, guided by a Qur’anic instruction (Surah al-Qasas: 7).
Notice “She was so sad, but she knew that Allah was much kinder to baby Moses than she was.” Her trust does not remove her sadness; the two stand together.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Killing Every Other Year”. How did the new policy work?
Listen once for the two decisions.
Read again and mark because, so and for fear that.
Open the picture hotspots “Killing Every Other Year” and “A Mother’s Trust” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: First five sentences: Find why the Pharaoh began to lose manpower and what his experts offered.
Middle: Find the year Moses was born in and what his mother did in secret.
Qur’anic quotation: Find the condition, the instruction, the comfort and the two promises.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: policy, carried out, realistic, grieve, experts.
“The Pharaoh thought the solution was economically realistic, so he accepted it.” What does the word realistic hide about the policy?
Write one sentence with policy and one with grieve.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the Pharaoh changed his order. Read the first five sentences of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the first five sentences.
Find what the economic experts warned the Pharaoh about.
Choose the option that names the reason in those sentences, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the new policy?
Can I contrast the Pharaoh’s reason with the mother’s?
Can I explain why for fear that fits and in case does not?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences about a difficult decision. Use one cause, one when or if condition, one instruction and one future reassurance, so that the sentences form a sequence.
content.reflectionPrompt: The Pharaoh spared boys for economic reasons, not mercy. How can a decision look kinder than it is when we do not ask why it was made?

objectives: I can explain how the baby came into the palace and why the queen wanted to keep him.
I can tell the queen’s persuasive hope from a fact the narrator proves.
I can report a request, a command and a contrast.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “would be” shows (Asiye’s hopeful prediction, reported from the past), then rewrite three sentences: the request with asked … to let her, the command with told … to find, and “unlike her husband” with whereas. The last activity asks you to write a persuasive proposal.
content.pronunciationFocus: Name: a-SI-ye. Stress: STER-ile, BE-liev-er, per-SUAD-ed. Read “Let me keep the baby and let him be our son.” as a gentle request, with stress on KEEP and SON.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Queen’s Wish”. What did the queen ask for? Listen once for the path of the basket and the queen’s response. Read again and mark the queen’s two direct sentences.
discussionPoints: The queen used words, not force, to protect a child inside a dangerous palace. When can gentle persuasion achieve more than open protest?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Carried by Calm Waves” and “A Queen’s Wish”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go to the middle of the chapter. Find the sentence that begins “She was always sad”. Use the Word Note for the key word, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short persuasive proposal for a new situation. Use Let me …, let … be …, and one sentence explaining why the proposal could benefit both sides.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the river to the palace to the waiting mother. Each step depends on a person’s response: the servants, the queen, the Pharaoh.

Notice “She was a secret believer and persuaded her husband with her words that this baby would be a ray of light for both of them!” Would be reports her hopeful prediction from the past, not a proven fact. The reference (see Surah al-Qasas: 9) points to the source.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Queen’s Wish”. What did the queen ask for?
Listen once for the path of the basket and the queen’s response.
Read again and mark the queen’s two direct sentences.
Open the picture hotspots “Carried by Calm Waves” and “A Queen’s Wish” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find what Allah commanded the waves and where the basket came to shore.
Middle: Find how the queen was different from her husband and why she was always sad.
Last sentences: Find her two requests and how Moses’ mother was waiting.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: ray of light, sterile, secret believer, wet nurse, with a heavy heart.
“While the queen was trying to choose a wet nurse to feed the baby, Moses’ mother was also waiting with a heavy heart.” Why does the writer put the two women in one sentence?
Write one sentence with secret believer and one with with a heavy heart.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the queen was always sad. Look in the middle of the chapter for a sentence with because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go to the middle of the chapter.
Find the sentence that begins “She was always sad”.
Use the Word Note for the key word, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain how the queen persuaded the Pharaoh?
Can I explain what would be shows here?
Can I report “Find a nurse for the baby.”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short persuasive proposal for a new situation. Use Let me …, let … be …, and one sentence explaining why the proposal could benefit both sides.
content.reflectionPrompt: The queen used words, not force, to protect a child inside a dangerous palace. When can gentle persuasion achieve more than open protest?

objectives: I can explain how Moses (pbuh) returned to his mother and grew up in the palace.
I can keep the timeline clear: This is before the prophetic mission.
I can describe an inner conflict with whether … or and had not yet.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide whether “He had not yet been given the prophetic mission.” means he was already a prophet, then correct three forms: whether he should (statement order), Because of + noun phrase, and had come. The last activity asks you to write about two competing duties.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: as-TON-ished, JUS-tice, pro-PHET-ic MIS-sion, op-POSE, NO-ble. Read the mother’s answer “I have sweet milk and a sweet scent, so no baby refuses me.” with calm confidence.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Prince Torn in Two”. What two duties pull at him? Listen once for the change from baby to young man. Read again and mark had not yet, whether … or, and Because of.
discussionPoints: Moses owed the Pharaoh his upbringing but saw the Pharaoh’s oppression. How should a person act when gratitude and justice point in different directions?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Back in His Mother’s Arms” and “A Prince Torn in Two”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find the sentence “Moses became a young man.” Read the next two sentences and find the verb that shows whether he had decided. Compare the statement with that verb, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–6 sentences about a person facing two competing duties. Use had not yet, whether … or, and one cause or result link.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two halves: The mother’s clever answer that brings the baby back to her, and the young man torn between gratitude and justice.
Notice “He had not yet been given the prophetic mission.” Everything Moses feels here belongs to the time before prophethood.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Prince Torn in Two”. What two duties pull at him?
Listen once for the change from baby to young man.
Read again and mark had not yet, whether … or, and Because of.
Open the picture hotspots “Back in His Mother’s Arms” and “A Prince Torn in Two” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find why the Pharaoh was astonished and how the mother answered.
Middle, just after Moses becomes a young man: Find the decision he could not make.
Last sentences: Find why the weak looked to him and why he felt close to the Israelites.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: astonished, justice, prophetic mission, oppose, noble.
“Young Moses felt close to the Israelites because he had come from the water, not from a noble family, and his mother was one of the Children of Israel.” Which two reasons does the sentence give?
Write one sentence with oppose and one with justice.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about what young Moses felt towards the Pharaoh. Read the middle of the chapter, just after he becomes a young man.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find the sentence “Moses became a young man.”
Read the next two sentences and find the verb that shows whether he had decided.
Compare the statement with that verb, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain how the baby returned to his mother?
Can I explain the young man’s conflict?
Can I correct “whether should he”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–6 sentences about a person facing two competing duties. Use had not yet, whether … or, and one cause or result link.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses owed the Pharaoh his upbringing but saw the Pharaoh’s oppression. How should a person act when gratitude and justice point in different directions?

objectives: I can explain what happened in the fight and what followed from it.
I can keep intention, consequence and the writer’s judgment apart.
I can rephrase intention, result and a warning.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort phrases into actions someone chose and consequences that followed, then rewrite three sentences: Unintentionally as did not mean to, results in as results from, and the warning “Run away, or the Pharaoh will kill you for this crime.” as an if-clause. The last activity asks you to write about a serious but unintended consequence.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: DIS-pute, un-in-TEN-tion-al-ly, QUAR-rel-some, un-REA-son-a-ble. Read the shout “Will you kill me just as you killed that Egyptian yesterday?” with rising fear, and the warning with urgency.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Single Punch”. Did Moses mean to kill? Listen once for the chain of events over two days. Read again and mark unintentionally, thus, So and was forced to.
discussionPoints: Moses turned to Allah for forgiveness immediately. Why does the speed of an apology matter, even when the harm was not intended?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Single Punch” and “Run Away!”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find “So Moses’ fear was not unreasonable.” Read the two sentences just before it. Choose the option built on those two facts, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 5-sentence claim and evidence explanation showing how a harmful consequence can be serious even when it was not intended. Use although or even though once.

whatToNotice: The chapter separates what Moses chose to do (he got involved and hit the man) from what followed (the death, the news, the flight).
Notice “So Moses’ fear was not unreasonable.” This is the writer’s judgment, built on the facts just before it. Not unreasonable is a careful, understated way of saying the fear was justified.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Single Punch”. Did Moses mean to kill?
Listen once for the chain of events over two days.
Read again and mark unintentionally, thus, So and was forced to.
Open the picture hotspots “A Single Punch” and “Run Away!” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find how Moses became involved and what happened to the Egyptian.
Middle: Find the next day’s dispute and what the Israelite shouted.
Last sentences: Find the warning from the man of faith and the Qur’anic account of the event.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: dispute, unintentionally, quarrelsome, death penalty, unreasonable.
“He unintentionally killed the Copt with a single punch.” How does one adverb change how you judge the act?
Write one sentence with dispute and one with quarrelsome.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks for the evidence behind the writer’s judgment about Moses’ fear. Find the sentence that begins “So Moses’ fear …” in the middle of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find “So Moses’ fear was not unreasonable.”
Read the two sentences just before it.
Choose the option built on those two facts, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what Moses chose and what followed?
Can I explain what not unreasonable means?
Can I turn the warning into an if-clause?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 5-sentence claim and evidence explanation showing how a harmful consequence can be serious even when it was not intended. Use although or even though once.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses turned to Allah for forgiveness immediately. Why does the speed of an apology matter, even when the harm was not intended?

objectives: I can explain how Moses’ repentance becomes a promise about the future.
I can tell Qur’anic words from the explanations added in brackets.
I can explain how context decides the meaning of a word such as plain.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four lines with what each does (admits a fault and asks for pardon, reports the answer, promises future conduct, accuses with a question about yesterday), then choose the meaning of plain in “Verily, you are a plain troublemaker!” (clear and obvious). The last activity asks you to move from a past mistake to a future commitment.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: TROU-ble-mak-er, CRIM-in-als, TY-rant, FA-vor. Read the prayer slowly and humbly, and the man’s question “O Moses! Is it your intention to kill me as you killed a man yesterday?” in a sharper, accusing voice.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Fault Admitted”. What does Moses admit? Listen once for the change from prayer to promise. Read again and mark each speaker: Moses, the narrator, and the man.
discussionPoints: Moses promised never to help wrongdoers again. Why is a promise about the future stronger than regret alone?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Fault Admitted” and “A Promise to Allah”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read Moses’ second saying again. Read the brackets: Who are the criminals here? Choose the option that matches that group, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–6 sentences about learning from a mistake. Move from what happened, to admitting it, to a future commitment with will not or will never.

whatToNotice: This chapter is a Qur’anic passage. It moves from admission to forgiveness, to a promise, and then to a new dispute the next day.

Notice “My Lord! Verily, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.” Moses names his fault before he asks for anything. The words in brackets after criminals are an explanation added by the translator, not part of the speech.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Fault Admitted”. What does Moses admit?
Listen once for the change from prayer to promise.
Read again and mark each speaker: Moses, the narrator, and the man.
Open the picture hotspots “A Fault Admitted” and “A Promise to Allah” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find Moses’ first prayer and the answer to it.
Moses’ second saying: Find his promise and the explanation in brackets.
Last sentences: Find what Moses called the man and what the man accused him of.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: troublemaker, criminals, seize, tyrant, favor.
“Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land, and not to be one of those who do right.” Whose accusation is this, and is it fair?
Write one sentence with favor and one with seize.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what Moses promises. Read his second saying at the start of the chapter and the explanation in brackets after “criminals”.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read Moses’ second saying again.
Read the brackets: Who are the criminals here?
Choose the option that matches that group, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the steps from admission to promise?
Can I explain what the brackets add?
Can I explain why plain means obvious here?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–6 sentences about learning from a mistake. Move from what happened, to admitting it, to a future commitment with will not or will never.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses promised never to help wrongdoers again. Why is a promise about the future stronger than regret alone?

objectives: I can follow Moses’ flight from the warning to the watering hole.
I can separate the practical reason for Midian, the physical risk and the inner trust.
I can use although, without + -ing and participle clauses to describe hardship.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four quoted lines with their meaning (the chiefs planning his death, a trustworthy warning, leaving while watching all around, a prayer for safety), then rewrite three sentences with Although, did not change and hid. The last activity asks you to describe a difficult journey.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: MID-i-an, SYR-i-a. Stress: IN-hab-it-ed, com-PAN-ion, pur-SUIT. Read “He traveled by night, hiding during the day.” with a pause at the comma, so the two parts balance.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Alone in the Desert”. How did Moses travel? Listen once and follow the journey from the city to Midian. Read again and mark every participle phrase (looking about, fearing pursuit, hiding during the day).
discussionPoints: Moses left with nothing prepared and kept going although his feet burned. What helps a person continue when a journey is harder than expected?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Warning from the City” and “Alone in the Desert”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the opening passage for the warning. Find how Moses left, how he traveled and where he stopped. Order the events again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–5 sentences about a difficult journey someone had to make. Use although or despite, one participle phrase such as fearing … or hoping …, and one sentence with without + -ing.

whatToNotice: The chapter begins with a Qur’anic passage (Surah al-Qasas: 15-21) and then continues in the narrator’s words.
Notice “His only companion in this hot desert was Allah and his trust in Him.” This is the narrator’s interpretation of the journey; the next sentences give the physical facts.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Alone in the Desert”. How did Moses travel?
Listen once and follow the journey from the city to Midian.
Read again and mark every participle phrase (looking about, fearing pursuit, hiding during the day).
Open the picture hotspots “A Warning from the City” and “Alone in the Desert” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find who warned Moses, what the chiefs were doing and Moses’ prayer.
Middle: Find how Moses left and why Midian was a safe goal.
Last sentences: Find the hardship on the way, how he traveled and where he arrived.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: taking counsel, watering hole, inhabited, companion, pursuit.
“Truly, I am to you one of those who give sincere advice.” Why does the man add this to his warning?
Write one sentence with inhabited and one with pursuit.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order four events of the flight. Start with the Qur’anic passage at the beginning and follow the journey to the last sentences.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the opening passage for the warning.
Find how Moses left, how he traveled and where he stopped.
Order the events again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why Midian was a good place to go?
Can I tell the narrator’s interpretation from the physical facts?
Can I rewrite a however contrast with although?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 4–5 sentences about a difficult journey someone had to make. Use although or despite, one participle phrase such as fearing … or hoping …, and one sentence with without + -ing.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses left with nothing prepared and kept going although his feet burned. What helps a person continue when a journey is harder than expected?

objectives: I can describe Moses’ condition when he reached Midian.
I can explain why the two women had to wait and why they were shepherding.
I can use could only … after, until and surprised that accurately.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “could only … after” shows (the women had to wait until the men had finished), then choose three forms: asked if he could, waiting until, and surprised that. The last activity asks you to interpret one phrase in the paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: ex-HAUST-ed, HARD-ship, TIRE-some, SHEP-herd-ing. Read the younger sister’s answer “Our father is an old man; his health is too poor and he cannot go out to shepherd the flock.” with a pause at the semicolon.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Worn Out by the Journey”. What had happened to his feet? Listen once for Moses’ needs and the women’s problem. Read again and mark noticed, sensed and was surprised.
discussionPoints: The women waited because the crowd came first. Who in your own surroundings has to wait until everyone else has finished, and what would help them?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Worn Out by the Journey” and “Two Sisters at the Well”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the opening sentences about his hunger and thirst. Then read the sentence where he approaches the women. Decide whether he had eaten and drunk first, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in 5–6 sentences why one phrase about Moses’ own need matters in the paragraph. Use one cause phrase, one limitation with could only, and one sentence of interpretation.

whatToNotice: The chapter first shows Moses’ own needs in detail (rest, sandals, food and drink) and only then the women’s difficulty. The order matters for what he does next.

Notice “Due to the crowd at the water source, the young women could only water their animals after the male shepherds had taken their flocks away.” The chapter gives a practical cause; it does not blame the other shepherds.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Worn Out by the Journey”. What had happened to his feet?
Listen once for Moses’ needs and the women’s problem.
Read again and mark noticed, sensed and was surprised.
Open the picture hotspots “Worn Out by the Journey” and “Two Sisters at the Well” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find Moses’ condition and what he urgently needed.
Middle: Find why the women had to wait and what Moses sensed.
Last sentences: Find what the older sister said, why Moses was surprised and the younger sister’s answer.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: exhausted, raw, hardship, flock, tiresome.
“Moses noticed their hardship and sensed that the women were in need of help.” What is the difference between noticing and sensing here?
Write one sentence with hardship and one with tiresome.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about when Moses offered help. Compare his condition at the beginning of the chapter with what he does in the middle.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the opening sentences about his hunger and thirst.
Then read the sentence where he approaches the women.
Decide whether he had eaten and drunk first, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I describe Moses’ condition?
Can I explain why the women had to wait?
Can I explain why until fits and during does not?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in 5–6 sentences why one phrase about Moses’ own need matters in the paragraph. Use one cause phrase, one limitation with could only, and one sentence of interpretation.
content.reflectionPrompt: The women waited because the crowd came first. Who in your own surroundings has to wait until everyone else has finished, and what would help them?

objectives: I can trace how Moses’ help leads to an invitation.
I can tell what Moses observes from the conclusion he draws.
I can use Due to, so that and After + -ing correctly.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide whether which in “which surprised their father” refers only to home, then correct three forms: Due to + a noun phrase (Moses’ help), so that for purpose, and After introducing. The last activity asks you to separate evidence from interpretation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Name: shu-AYB, the GULF of AQ-a-ba. Stress: har-MO-ni-ous, un-FOR-tu-nate, un-ex-PECT-ed-ly. Read “He suddenly realized he hadn’t drunk any water.” with stress on SUD-den-ly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “An Invitation from Shu’ayb”. Why was Moses invited? Listen once for the chain from help to invitation. Read again and mark which surprised their father, Due to and so that.
discussionPoints: Moses helped strangers without asking for anything and found a home. How does helping without expecting a reward change the person who helps?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Help at the Spring” and “An Invitation from Shu’ayb”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find where the daughter goes up to Moses. Read what she says her father wants to do. Choose the option that matches her words, not a later event, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Using the sentence about the family’s home life, write 4–5 sentences that separate what Moses directly observes from the interpretation he forms.

whatToNotice: The event order supports a reading of selflessness: Moses waters the sheep, sits down, and only then realizes he has not drunk anything himself.
Notice “It was clear to Moses that they enjoyed a comfortable and harmonious home life.” This is Moses’ interpretation of what he sees, reported by the narrator.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “An Invitation from Shu’ayb”. Why was Moses invited?
Listen once for the chain from help to invitation.
Read again and mark which surprised their father, Due to and so that.
Open the picture hotspots “Help at the Spring” and “An Invitation from Shu’ayb” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find what Moses did and what he realized afterward.
Middle: Find who the father was, where he was sent, and why he sent his daughters alone.
Second half: Find why the daughters came home early and the daughter’s exact words to Moses.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: harmonious, in person, unfortunate, grateful, unexpectedly.
“The young ladies returned home unexpectedly early, which surprised their father.” What does which refer to?
Write one sentence with grateful and one with in person.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the father sent one of his daughters. Read the second half of the chapter and find the daughter’s exact words.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find where the daughter goes up to Moses.
Read what she says her father wants to do.
Choose the option that matches her words, not a later event, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I retell the events in order?
Can I explain what which refers to?
Can I tell what Moses sees from what he concludes?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Using the sentence about the family’s home life, write 4–5 sentences that separate what Moses directly observes from the interpretation he forms.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses helped strangers without asking for anything and found a home. How does helping without expecting a reward change the person who helps?

objectives: I can explain the reasons behind each decision in Midian.
I can explain why the chapter calls the ten years a preparation, not a delay.
I can use advise, offer and marry with the right patterns.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the reason the offer suited Moses, correct three verb patterns (advised her father to employ, offered Moses work, married one of the daughters), then complete a line with for, After and during. The last activity asks you to argue that the ten years were preparation, not delay.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: SI-nai, RAM-seez. Stress: GEN-tle-ness, em-PLOY, re-LI-a-ble, SHEL-ter. Read the dates as twelve seventy-nine to twelve thirteen BC.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Preparing for Prophethood”. How did the quiet years help him? Listen once and follow Moses from guest to shepherd. Read again and mark every reason word: for, Because, because.
discussionPoints: Ten quiet years looking after animals prepared Moses for leadership. How can ordinary, patient work prepare someone for a bigger task later?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Ten Years in Midian” and “Preparing for Prophethood”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one question at a time. Find the reason word near the decision it explains. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–7 sentences explaining why the text calls the ten years spiritual preparation rather than a delay. Use two pieces of chapter evidence and one framing phrase such as the chapter presents ….

whatToNotice: Almost every decision in the chapter comes with a stated reason: for …, Because …, because ….
Notice “It was a period of spiritual preparation for prophethood.” The events are ordinary (work, family, thought); the meaning of the ten years is the chapter’s interpretation.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Preparing for Prophethood”. How did the quiet years help him?
Listen once and follow Moses from guest to shepherd.
Read again and mark every reason word: for, Because, because.
Open the picture hotspots “Ten Years in Midian” and “Preparing for Prophethood” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find how the old man comforted Moses and why Moses felt at home.
Middle: Find why a daughter advised her father and why the offer suited Moses.
Last sentences: Find how long Moses stayed, what the period meant and when he returned.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: comfort, gentleness, employ, shelter, reliable.
“Because they needed someone reliable and strong, one of the daughters advised her father to employ Moses.” What had the family seen that showed these qualities?
Write one sentence with reliable and one with shelter.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four questions with the reasons the chapter gives. Look for the words for, because and important.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one question at a time.
Find the reason word near the decision it explains.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I give the reason for each decision?
Can I explain why the ten years were a preparation?
Can I correct “advised her father employing”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–7 sentences explaining why the text calls the ten years spiritual preparation rather than a delay. Use two pieces of chapter evidence and one framing phrase such as the chapter presents ….
content.reflectionPrompt: Ten quiet years looking after animals prepared Moses for leadership. How can ordinary, patient work prepare someone for a bigger task later?

content.chapter: Chapter 15: The Voice at Mount Sinai
objectives: I can follow the change from an ordinary winter night to the start of Moses’ mission.
I can tell the narrated events from the writer’s explanation of them.
I can use hoping to, so that and was about to.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “hoping to” shows (a result he wanted but could not yet be sure of), then rewrite a purpose infinitive as a so that clause and was about to happen with was going to. The last activity asks you to describe the move from ordinary to extraordinary.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: SI-nai, TUR. Stress: NIGHT-fall, THUN-der-ing, TREM-ble, TWIST-ing. Read the voice’s question “And what is in your right hand, O Moses?” slowly, and Moses’ answer as a simple, shaken reply.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Fire in the Distance”. Why did Moses walk towards the fire? Listen once for the ordinary purpose and the unexpected voice. Read again and mark what the narrator explains between the voice’s words.
discussionPoints: Moses went looking for warmth and directions and found his life’s mission. Why do important turning points often begin in ordinary moments?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Fire in the Distance” and “The Staff Becomes a Snake”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find Moses’ answer about the staff. Read the next two sentences, where the writer explains. Choose the option that matches the writer’s explanation, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences describing how the chapter moves from the ordinary uses of the staff to its extraordinary role. Use at first, then, and one relative clause with which or on which.

whatToNotice: The chapter begins with ordinary needs: A lost way, a cold night, fire for warmth, a guide. The turning point comes out of these ordinary purposes.
Notice “This was the beginning of Moses’ mission as a prophet.” The narrator stops the scene to name its meaning; compare this with Chapter 8, where the mission had not yet begun.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Fire in the Distance”. Why did Moses walk towards the fire?
Listen once for the ordinary purpose and the unexpected voice.
Read again and mark what the narrator explains between the voice’s words.
Open the picture hotspots “A Fire in the Distance” and “The Staff Becomes a Snake” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find the season, the problem on the way and the other name of the mountain.
Middle: Find why Moses approached the fire and what the voice asked him.
After Moses answers: Find the writer’s explanation, then the staff and the snake.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: nightfall, thundering, tremble, staff, twisting.
“This is my staff on which I lean, and I use it to cut branches for my sheep.” Why does Moses describe such ordinary uses?
Write one sentence with tremble and one with nightfall.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why, according to the writer, Allah asked about the staff. Read the sentences right after Moses answers “This is my staff …”.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find Moses’ answer about the staff.
Read the next two sentences, where the writer explains.
Choose the option that matches the writer’s explanation, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the ordinary reasons for approaching the fire?
Can I point to the narrator’s explanation?
Can I rewrite was about to happen?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences describing how the chapter moves from the ordinary uses of the staff to its extraordinary role. Use at first, then, and one relative clause with which or on which.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses went looking for warmth and directions and found his life’s mission. Why do important turning points often begin in ordinary moments?

objectives: I can explain the two signs and the command that follows them.
I can see that the Qur’anic passage goes back to the scene at the fire.
I can shorten a reason into a participle clause and report a command.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four lines from the fire scene with what they do (a request to wait, a hopeful possibility, an instruction with its reason, a consequence of the declaration), then rewrite the because-clause with Realizing and report the command with commanded Moses to go. The last activity asks you to explain how the signs change Moses’ situation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Name: TU-wa. Stress: sub-SIDE, WIT-ness, ex-CEP-tion-al-ly, SA-cred. Read “So take off your shoes; you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa.” with a pause at the semicolon, then give the reason clearly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Shining Hand”. What was the second sign? Listen once for signs, command and the return to the fire. Read again and mark the reasons: because, for, and the reason after the semicolon.
discussionPoints: Moses received two great signs and, with them, a hard task. When does receiving a gift or ability also bring a responsibility?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Shining Hand” and “The Valley of Tuwa”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the first two sentences again. Find what happened to his fear and the word that introduces the reason. Compare the statement with those words, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences explaining how receiving the two signs changes Moses’ situation. Include one cause clause, one reported command and one purpose clause.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two parts: The narrator’s account of the signs and the command, then “Allah narrated this event” with a Qur’anic passage that returns to the moment at the fire.
Notice “You have two signs from your Lord; go to Pharaoh and his chiefs, for they are an evil group and have violated all limits.” The signs are followed at once by a task; for here means because.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Shining Hand”. What was the second sign?
Listen once for signs, command and the return to the fire.
Read again and mark the reasons: because, for, and the reason after the semicolon.
Open the picture hotspots “The Shining Hand” and “The Valley of Tuwa” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: First two sentences: Find what happened to the staff and to Moses’ fear.
Middle: Find the second sign and the command to go to Pharaoh.
Qur’anic passage: Find what Moses told his family, why he had to take off his shoes, and the call to worship.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: subside, witness, exceptionally, chiefs, sacred.
“perhaps I can bring you some burning brand therefrom, or find some guidance at the fire.” Why does Moses say perhaps?
Write one sentence with subside and one with sacred.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about Moses’ fear and its reason. Read the first two sentences of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the first two sentences again.
Find what happened to his fear and the word that introduces the reason.
Compare the statement with those words, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name the two signs?
Can I explain what the Qur’anic passage adds?
Can I report the command with to go?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences explaining how receiving the two signs changes Moses’ situation. Include one cause clause, one reported command and one purpose clause.
content.reflectionPrompt: Moses received two great signs and, with them, a hard task. When does receiving a gift or ability also bring a responsibility?

objectives: I can explain the warning and the signs in the Qur’anic passage.
I can explain the writer’s claim of continuity from Abraham to Moses.
I can use lest, the same as that of, and one of + plural noun.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the meaning of “lest you fall” (so that you do not fall), then choose three forms: the same as that of, one of the descendants and one of Abraham’s successors. The last activity asks you to explain the chapter’s claim of continuity.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: TA-ha, A-bra-ham, JA-cob. Stress: MON-o-the-ism, de-SCEND-ant, suc-CES-sor, FOR-mer. Read “Go to Pharaoh!” as a strong command, and the family line slowly, one name at a time.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “In Abraham’s Line”. How are Jacob and Abraham related? Listen once for the warning, the signs and the command. Read the last three sentences again and mark therefore.
discussionPoints: The chapter says that the same belief was passed on from prophet to prophet. What makes an idea continue across many generations?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Go to Pharaoh!” and “In Abraham’s Line”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find (Surah Taha: 9-24). Read the three sentences after it and draw the line Abraham, Jacob, Moses. Choose the option that fits your line and the word religion, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences explaining the chapter’s claim of prophetic continuity from Abraham through Jacob to Moses. Use one relative clause and one consequence connector such as therefore.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two parts: A long Qur’anic passage (Surah Taha: 9-24), then three sentences in the writer’s own voice about family and belief.

Notice that Moses’ answer about the stick is worded differently from Chapter 15: “This is my stick, I lean on it, and with it I beat down branches for my sheep and I find other uses in it.” The same event is told in a different translation.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “In Abraham’s Line”. How are Jacob and Abraham related?
Listen once for the warning, the signs and the command.
Read the last three sentences again and mark therefore.
Open the picture hotspots “Go to Pharaoh!” and “In Abraham’s Line” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening lines: Find why the Hour is kept hidden and the warning that follows.
Middle: Find the two signs and why they are given.
Last three sentences, after the surah reference: Find how Moses, Jacob and Abraham are connected.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: monotheism, descendant, successor, desires, former.

“Moses (pbuh), therefore, was one of the descendants of Abraham (pbuh), and every prophet who came after Abraham (pbuh) was one of Abraham’s successors.” What is the difference between a descendant and a successor?
Write one sentence with former and one with desires.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks for the main point of the last part of the chapter. Read the last three sentences, after the surah reference.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find (Surah Taha: 9-24).
Read the three sentences after it and draw the line Abraham, Jacob, Moses.
Choose the option that fits your line and the word religion, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the two signs?
Can I explain what therefore shows?
Can I explain why that of is needed?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5 sentences explaining the chapter’s claim of prophetic continuity from Abraham through Jacob to Moses. Use one relative clause and one consequence connector such as therefore.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says that the same belief was passed on from prophet to prophet. What makes an idea continue across many generations?

objectives: I can explain what Moses and Aaron asked for and how the Pharaoh answered.
I can explain how the Pharaoh’s questions put pressure on Moses.
I can move between direct and reported questions.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four questions with what each does in the dialogue (demands a request, refuses through a claim of ownership, presents a claim as obvious, uses Moses’ past as pressure), rewrite reported and direct questions (Is your name, did you find, wanted), then choose the contrast the exchange builds. The last activity asks you to analyse two questions.
content.pronunciationFocus: Name: AA-ron. Stress: de-LIV-er, CHAR-i-ty, per-MIS-sion, de-FENSE-less, MOCK-ing-ly. Read “Their Lord is Allah.” calmly and firmly, after the Pharaoh’s louder question.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Two Brothers, One Message”. Who helped Moses? Listen once for the request and the refusal. Read again and mark every question and who asks it.
discussionPoints: The Pharaoh reminded Moses of the food and charity he had received. Can past kindness ever give someone the right to silence you?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Two Brothers, One Message” and “They Are My Slaves”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find “Their Lord is Allah.” Read the question that comes just before it. Ask what claim that question makes, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Choose two questions from the chapter and explain in 5–6 sentences how each one tries to control the dialogue. Use whereas or while to compare their functions.

whatToNotice: The dialogue is a contest of claims: Ownership against lordship. Most of the Pharaoh’s lines are questions that are not real requests for information.
Notice “Didn’t he know that the Pharaoh was a god?” The narrator voices the Pharaoh’s view here; it is his claim, not the narrator’s belief.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Two Brothers, One Message”. Who helped Moses?
Listen once for the request and the refusal.
Read again and mark every question and who asks it.
Open the picture hotspots “Two Brothers, One Message” and “They Are My Slaves” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find who Aaron was and what Moses told the Pharaoh about.
Middle: Find what Moses wanted and the Pharaoh’s reply about the Israelites.
Last sentences: Find how the Pharaoh used Moses’ past as a baby and in the palace.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: deliver, charity, permission, defenseless, mockingly.
“Aren’t you that Moses who we raised in our palace, who ate our food, upon whom our charity and wealth were showered?” What does the Pharaoh want Moses to feel?
Write one sentence with permission and one with defenseless.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks which of the Pharaoh’s claims Moses rejects. Read the Pharaoh’s question just before “Their Lord is Allah.” in the middle of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find “Their Lord is Allah.”
Read the question that comes just before it.
Ask what claim that question makes, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain Moses’ request?
Can I explain why the Pharaoh’s questions are not neutral?
Can I turn a reported question into a direct one?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Choose two questions from the chapter and explain in 5–6 sentences how each one tries to control the dialogue. Use whereas or while to compare their functions.
content.reflectionPrompt: The Pharaoh reminded Moses of the food and charity he had received. Can past kindness ever give someone the right to silence you?

objectives: I can trace the move from accusation to threat to sign.
I can tell the Pharaoh’s accusation from Moses’ answer as the narrator reports it.
I can use rather, despite the fact that and have no choice but to.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter into the Pharaoh’s accusation in his own words and Moses’ reported answer, rewrite a concession with although, a “What if …?” challenge and a threat with threatened to imprison, then correct rather and to display. The last activity asks you to write a structured rebuttal.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: UP-bring-ing, im-PRIS-on, re-VENGE, con-VINC-ing, O-pen-ly. Read “If you accept any god other than me, I will imprison you!” with rising force, and “What if I bring you something convincing and true?” calmly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Past Brought Up”. What did the Pharaoh remind Moses of? Listen once for the three stages. Read again and mark rather, despite the fact that, and had no choice but.
discussionPoints: When his arguments failed, the Pharaoh turned to threats. What does it tell you when someone answers evidence with a threat?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Past Brought Up” and “A Threat of Prison”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the opening accusation and Moses’ answers. Find the point where the discussions stop working. Put the threat, the offer and the staff after it, then order again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 6-sentence rebuttal in a new context. Use rather, despite, one if-clause and What if …? to move from correction to challenge.

whatToNotice: The Pharaoh speaks directly and in the present; Moses’ answer is reported by the narrator (he explained that …). The form tells you who is speaking.

Notice “Moses (pbuh) knew that Pharaoh’s talk about his past, his upbringing, and the Pharaoh’s charity was his way of threatening him.” The narrator tells you how to read the Pharaoh’s words: as a threat, not a discussion.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Past Brought Up”. What did the Pharaoh remind Moses of?
Listen once for the three stages.
Read again and mark rather, despite the fact that, and had no choice but.
Open the picture hotspots “The Past Brought Up” and “A Threat of Prison” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find the Pharaoh’s accusation and how the narrator explains it.
Middle: Find Moses’ three answers and what the intellectual discussions led to.
Last sentences: Find the threat, Moses’ offer and what happened to the staff.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: upbringing, imprison, revenge, convincing, openly.
“After long dialogues, Moses (pbuh) understood that the intellectual discussions did not work.” What changes when words stop working?
Write one sentence with revenge and one with convincing.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will order five events of the meeting. Follow the chapter from the Pharaoh’s accusation at the start to the staff at the very end.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the opening accusation and Moses’ answers.
Find the point where the discussions stop working.
Put the threat, the offer and the staff after it, then order again.
selfCheck: Can I name the three stages?
Can I tell the Pharaoh’s words from Moses’ reported answer?
Can I explain why rather fits better than however?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 6-sentence rebuttal in a new context. Use rather, despite, one if-clause and What if …? to move from correction to challenge.
content.reflectionPrompt: When his arguments failed, the Pharaoh turned to threats. What does it tell you when someone answers evidence with a threat?

objectives: I can explain the advisors’ plan and its political purpose.
I can tell the narrator’s judgment from what things seemed to be.
I can rephrase a decision, a recommendation and a motive.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four expressions with their meaning in context (eager to watch, lessen the impact, make him fail in his claim, only an illusion), then rewrite three sentences: The passive decision as an active one with to hold, the recommendation with detaining, and “out of fear that” with because he feared. The last activity asks you to explain how the advisors try to manage public perception.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: ash-shu-A-ra. Stress: BRIGHT-ness, de-TAIN, IM-pact, ad-VI-sors, il-LU-sion. Read “It was a hand that shed light!” with wonder, and “However, this was only an illusion.” with stress on ON-ly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Plan Against the Signs”. What did the advisors suggest? Listen once for the plan and what the magicians did. Read again and mark It was decided that, might, aimed to and only.
discussionPoints: The advisors wanted to control what the people believed about the signs. How can you tell when someone is trying to manage your opinion rather than inform it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Plan Against the Signs” and “Ropes Like Snakes”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find the advisors’ recommendation. Read the sentence that begins “In this way”. Choose the option that matches their aim, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences explaining how the advisors plan to reduce the impact of Moses’ signs. Use one passive reporting structure, one purpose expression, and one sentence showing expectation versus outcome.

whatToNotice: The contest is not a neutral test. Its aim is stated openly: To lessen the effect of the miracles on the people and make Moses fail.

Notice “These two miracles by Prophet Moses (pbuh) actually demonstrated his prophethood.” Actually shows the narrator’s stance. At the end, “However, this was only an illusion.” uses only to reduce the magicians’ snakes to appearance.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Plan Against the Signs”. What did the advisors suggest?
Listen once for the plan and what the magicians did.
Read again and mark It was decided that, might, aimed to and only.
Open the picture hotspots “A Plan Against the Signs” and “Ropes Like Snakes” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find the white hand and what the two miracles demonstrated.
Middle, after the advisors speak: Find what they recommended and what they aimed to do.
Last sentences: Find what the crowd and the magicians wanted, and what the magicians’ staffs and ropes really were.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: brightness, detain, impact, advisors, illusion.
“But things did not go as the Pharaoh had expected.” Why does the writer tell you this before the contest has even begun?
Write one sentence with impact and one with detain.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the advisors wanted the cleverest magicians. Read the middle of the chapter after the advisors speak, and find the sentence that begins “In this way …”.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find the advisors’ recommendation.
Read the sentence that begins “In this way”.
Choose the option that matches their aim, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the political purpose of the contest?
Can I explain what actually and only show?
Can I rewrite “It was decided that …” in the active?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences explaining how the advisors plan to reduce the impact of Moses’ signs. Use one passive reporting structure, one purpose expression, and one sentence showing expectation versus outcome.
content.reflectionPrompt: The advisors wanted to control what the people believed about the signs. How can you tell when someone is trying to manage your opinion rather than inform it?

objectives: I can explain why the magicians’ belief was a major defeat for the Pharaoh.
I can compare the experts’ recognition with the people’s obedience.
I can use not merely … but, since, and -ed and -ing adjectives accurately.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “not merely … but” adds (why the magicians’ belief carried weight), correct three forms (couldn’t do anything but advise, After seeing, since + clause), then choose horrified and ordering. The last activity asks you to compare expert recognition with public obedience.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: e-LITE, dis-ap-POINT-ment, re-spon-si-BIL-i-ty, cor-RUPT, SUB-jects. Read “We believe in the Lord of Moses and Aaron.” slowly and clearly, as a public declaration.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Blind Obedience”. Why did many people ignore Moses? Listen once and count the different responses. Read again and mark So, since and not merely … but.
discussionPoints: The people ignored Moses because the Pharaoh met their material needs. What can make people accept injustice from someone who feeds them?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Bowing Down to Allah” and “Blind Obedience”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one person or group at a time. Find the sentence where that person or group acts or speaks. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–8 sentences explaining why the experts’ recognition damages the Pharaoh’s position while many ordinary subjects still obey him. Use not merely … but, so, and one cause connector.

whatToNotice: One event produces four responses: The magicians believe, the Pharaoh’s ministers fear losing power, Moses advises patience, and many people keep obeying the Pharaoh.
Notice “At that time, magicians were not merely performers, but the elite intellectual scholars of ancient Egypt.” This explanation from the writer shows why their belief mattered so much.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Blind Obedience”. Why did many people ignore Moses?
Listen once and count the different responses.
Read again and mark So, since and not merely … but.
Open the picture hotspots “Bowing Down to Allah” and “Blind Obedience” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Opening sentences: Find what the illusion did to Moses for a moment and what his staff did.
Middle: Find what the magicians said and how the Pharaoh and his prime minister reacted.
Last sentences: Find what the Pharaoh did at the large assembly and why the people obeyed him.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: elite, disappointment, responsibility, corrupt, subjects.
“They lacked vision since they had been under oppression for a long time.” Is this a fact the narrator reports or an explanation the writer gives?
Write one sentence with elite and one with subjects.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four people or groups with what they did. Read from the magicians’ words in the first half to the large assembly at the end.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one person or group at a time.
Find the sentence where that person or group acts or speaks.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the magicians’ belief mattered?
Can I explain why many people still obeyed?
Can I explain horrified and horrifying?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–8 sentences explaining why the experts’ recognition damages the Pharaoh’s position while many ordinary subjects still obey him. Use not merely … but, so, and one cause connector.
content.reflectionPrompt: The people ignored Moses because the Pharaoh met their material needs. What can make people accept injustice from someone who feeds them?

objectives: I can follow the escape from the night departure to the crossing.
I can separate what the people could see, what Moses said, and what happened next.
I can move between participle clauses and full clauses.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort lines into fear of the visible danger and trust before a way is visible, rewrite two sentences with participle and full clauses (Realizing their departure, because they found no other way), then choose managed to catch and parted. The last activity asks you to analyse certainty before visible evidence.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: GEN-o-cide, MO-bi-lize, PAN-ic, in-HER-it, EX-o-dus. Read “We are sure to be caught up with.” with fear, then “Truly! With me is my Lord; He will guide me.” with calm certainty.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Escape by Night”. Why did they leave at night? Listen once and follow the time words: at night, When the sun rose, Soon, Then. Read again and mark the two kinds of certainty: About the danger and about guidance.
discussionPoints: Moses spoke with confidence before the sea opened. What is the difference between trust and simply ignoring danger?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Escape by Night” and “A Path Through the Sea”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read paragraph 2 for the departure. Read paragraph 3 and mark When the sun rose, Soon and Then. Order the events again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 6–8 sentences analysing the difference between the people’s visible evidence and Moses’ confidence. Keep separate what the characters can see, what Moses says, and what happens later.

whatToNotice: This chapter has four paragraphs. Paragraphs 1–3 tell the story; the Qur’anic passage begins at the end of paragraph 3 and continues in paragraph 4.
Notice “However, Moses (pbuh) said that Allah was with them and would show them the way to safety”. Moses speaks with confidence before any path is visible; the sea parts only afterwards.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Escape by Night”. Why did they leave at night?
Listen once and follow the time words: at night, When the sun rose, Soon, Then.

content.chapter: Chapter 24: The Calf and the Torah
objectives: I can explain what happened after the escape: The request for an idol, the Torah and the calf.

content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the story and the writer’s framing, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.

metadata.title: Moses B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Judge • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the story of Prophet Moses (pbuh) on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the story and the writer’s framing across the 24 chapters.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Tell sources, Qur’anic passages and characters’ claims from the writer’s interpretation.
Use qualified language when the evidence is qualified.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text, not with guesses.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 24.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the story and the writer’s framing.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for what happens, once to follow the exact wording.
points: First listening: What happens, and what does the writer say it means?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Most chapters are one long paragraph: Pause after every three or four sentences and say what has changed.
Replay one long sentence or Qur’anic line and read it with the same pauses and stress.

sections.title: 3. Evidence or Interpretation?
sections.text: This book mixes history, Qur’anic passages, reports, characters’ claims and the writer’s own interpretation. Learn to tell them apart.
points: History from sources is framed: According to the sources …, probably, approximately, is unknown (Chapter 2).
A Qur’anic passage or report has a reference or a name: (Surah al-Qasas: 7), Ibn Abbas said … (Chapters 5, 6).
A character’s claim belongs to the speaker: The Pharaoh’s “my slaves” and “at my command” are his words, not facts (Chapters 18, 23).
An interpretation says what events mean: Apparently …, It is possible that …, a period of spiritual preparation (Chapters 3, 5, 14).
Keep your own claims as careful as the evidence.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five Word Notes (six in Chapters 22 and 23) and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to work out the meaning yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Use the word in a sentence that explains a cause, a contrast or a choice.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Answer the Quick Challenge before reading the feedback. Then do the three or four Language Focus activities.
points: First activity (Notice): See what a sentence or phrase does in the story.
Middle activities (Build): choose, correct, sort or rewrite forms from the chapter.
Last activity (Use): Write a B2 response of your own, often about a different situation.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work in chunks of three or four sentences.
Write a one-line summary of each chunk.
Mark events, sources, speakers’ claims and interpretations in different colors.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The story of Moses (pbuh) contrasts tyranny with trust, service and determination. Connect each value to one action.
points: Trust with action: Act on guidance even when you are afraid (Chapters 6, 22).
Responsibility: Admit a wrong at once and change your future conduct (Chapters 9, 10).
Service: Help people in need before your own comfort, without asking for a reward (Chapters 12, 13).
Courage before power: Speak the truth calmly to someone who threatens you (Chapters 18, 19).
Honesty with evidence: Accept the truth when you see it, as the magicians did, instead of twisting it, as the Pharaoh did (Chapters 21, 23).
Determination: Keep guiding and serving even when people do not change quickly (Chapter 24).
